"'''Cathy's Clown'''" is a [[popular music|popular]] [[song]], written by [[Don Everly]] and recorded by [[The Everly Brothers]] in 1960. The lyrics describe a man who has been wronged and publicly humiliated by his lover: "Here he comes / That's Cathy's clown". The choruses are sung by brothers Don and Phil in their trademark [[close harmony]] style, while Don sings the bridges solo.

"Cathy's Clown" is noted for its unorthodox structure, such as beginning on a [[Song structure#Chorus or refrain|chorus]] and having [[Bridge (music)|bridge]]s but no [[Song structure#Verse|verses]]. The song was a worldwide success and the best-selling single of the Everly Brothers' career. Because of its enduring influence on popular music, the song was added to the [[National Recording Registry]] of the [[Library of Congress]] in 2013.<ref name=Levitin2013>Daniel J. Levitin (2013) [http://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/CathysClown.pdf The Everly Brothers - Cathy's Clown]. Library of Congress, accessed 12 Jan 2020</ref>

"Cathy's Clown" is a popular song, written by Don Everly and recorded by The Everly Brothers in 1960. The lyrics describe a man who has been wronged and publicly humiliated by his lover: "Here he comes / That's Cathy's clown". The choruses are sung by brothers Don and Phil in their trademark close harmony style, while Don sings the bridges solo.

"Cathy's Clown" is noted for its unorthodox structure, such as beginning on a chorus and having bridges but no verses. The song was a worldwide success and the best-selling single of the Everly Brothers' career. Because of its enduring influence on popular music, the song was added to the National Recording Registry of the Library of Congress in 2013.

sections.heading: Recording
sections.wikitext: The musicians included the Everlys and Hank Garland on guitars, [[Floyd Cramer]] on piano, [[Floyd Chance]] on bass and [[Buddy Harman]] on drums.  The distinctive drum sound was achieved by recording them with a tape loop, making it sound as if there were two drummers.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://forums.stevehoffman.tv/threads/recording-the-everly-brothers-cathys-clown.12542/ |title=Recording The Everly Brothers' "Cathy's Clown" | Steve Hoffman Music Forums |website=Forums.stevehoffman.tv |access-date=2016-08-29}}</ref> "Cathy's Clown" was recorded live in a single take, with Don and Phil sharing a microphone.<ref name=Levitin2013/>
sections.text: The musicians included the Everlys and Hank Garland on guitars, Floyd Cramer on piano, Floyd Chance on bass and Buddy Harman on drums.  The distinctive drum sound was achieved by recording them with a tape loop, making it sound as if there were two drummers. "Cathy's Clown" was recorded live in a single take, with Don and Phil sharing a microphone.

sections.heading: History
sections.wikitext:
[[File:Cathy's Clown - Always It's You ad - Cash Box 1960.jpg|thumb|160px|''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' advertisement, April 9 1960]] 
"Cathy's Clown" was The Everly Brothers' first single for Warner Bros., having previously recorded for [[Archie Bleyer]]'s [[Cadence Records|Cadence label]] for three years. It sold eight million copies worldwide, spending five weeks at number 1 on the U.S. [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] chart and one week on the R&B chart.<ref>{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942–2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=194}}</ref> The song spent seven weeks at number 1 on the [[UK Singles Chart]] in May and June 1960,<ref name="500 Number One Hits">{{cite book
| first= Jo
| last= Rice
| year= 1982
| title= The Guinness Book of 500 Number One Hits
| publisher= Guinness Superlatives 
| location= Enfield, Middlesex
| page= 50
| isbn= 0-85112-250-7}}</ref> and was the Everly Brothers' biggest-selling single and their third and final U.S. number 1 hit. ''Billboard'' ranked it as the number 3 song of the year for 1960.<ref>[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1960]]</ref>

In 2004, it was ranked 149th on ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' magazine's list of the [[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|500 Greatest Songs of All Time]].

In November 2018, a judge ruled that Don was the sole writer of "Cathy's Clown", as Phil had relinquished his rights sometime before June 1980. [[Acuff-Rose Music]], which owned the song publishing, and [[Broadcast Music, Inc.|BMI]] (the brothers' rights society) removed Phil's name from all the royalty statements. In 2011, Don filed to regain ownership, with the estate of Phil following in 2014.<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=http://www.billboard.com/articles/business/8486916/everly-brothers-cathys-clown-songwriting-credit-royalties|title=Everly Brothers at Odds in Case Over Lucrative 'Cathy's Clown' Royalties|date=November 28, 2018|magazine=Billboard}}</ref>
sections.text:
thumb|160px|[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox advertisement, April 9 1960]] 
"Cathy's Clown" was The Everly Brothers' first single for Warner Bros., having previously recorded for Archie Bleyer's Cadence label for three years. It sold eight million copies worldwide, spending five weeks at number 1 on the U.S. Billboard Hot 100 chart and one week on the R&B chart. The song spent seven weeks at number 1 on the UK Singles Chart in May and June 1960, and was the Everly Brothers' biggest-selling single and their third and final U.S. number 1 hit. Billboard ranked it as the number 3 song of the year for 1960.

In 2004, it was ranked 149th on Rolling Stone magazine's list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time.

In November 2018, a judge ruled that Don was the sole writer of "Cathy's Clown", as Phil had relinquished his rights sometime before June 1980. Acuff-Rose Music, which owned the song publishing, and BMI (the brothers' rights society) removed Phil's name from all the royalty statements. In 2011, Don filed to regain ownership, with the estate of Phil following in 2014.

sections.heading: Associations
sections.wikitext:
"Cathy's Clown" was inspired by [[Ferde Grofé]]'s ''[[Grand Canyon Suite]]''.<ref name="bbc2014"/> It was a major influence on the [[The Beatles|Beatles]], who — having "once toyed with calling themselves The Foreverly Brothers" — three years later copied the Everly's harmonies on their first U.K. No. 1 hit single, "[[Please Please Me (song)|Please Please Me]]".<ref name="bbc2014">{{cite news| title= The Everly Brothers: 'That Sibling Sound'| url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-25608321| first=Mark |last=Savage | work= BBC News | date= 4 January 2014| access-date= 2014-01-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| last=MacDonald| first=Ian| year=2005| author-link= Ian MacDonald| title=Revolution in the Head: The Beatles' Records and the Sixties| page=62| publisher= Pimlico (Rand)| location=London| edition=2nd rev.| isbn=1-84413-828-3}}</ref>

"Cathy's Clown" is mentioned in the [[Opening sentence|opening line]] of [[Elliott Smith]]'s song "Waltz 2 (XO)", the title track of his 1998 album ''[[XO (Elliott Smith album)|XO]]''.<ref>{{cite web| url= http://www.musicsonglyrics.com/waltz--2-xo-lyrics-elliott-smith.html | title= Elliott Smith "Waltz 2 (XO)" lyrics | publisher= musicsonglyrics.com | access-date= 2014-01-06}}</ref>

[[Jan and Dean]] recorded a cover of "Cathy's Clown" for their album ''Filet of Soul'', but [[Liberty Records]] rejected both track listings that included the song. Liberty later selected its own track listing, which did not include "Cathy's Clown", and released it shortly after Jan Berry's crash near Deadman's Curve. Jan & Dean's cover of "Cathy's Clown" is available on the "Filet Of Soul Redux: The Rejected Master Recordings" release.
sections.text:
"Cathy's Clown" was inspired by Ferde Grofé's Grand Canyon Suite. It was a major influence on the Beatles, who — having "once toyed with calling themselves The Foreverly Brothers" — three years later copied the Everly's harmonies on their first U.K. No. 1 hit single, "Please Please Me".

"Cathy's Clown" is mentioned in the opening line of Elliott Smith's song "Waltz 2 (XO)", the title track of his 1998 album XO.

Jan and Dean recorded a cover of "Cathy's Clown" for their album Filet of Soul, but Liberty Records rejected both track listings that included the song. Liberty later selected its own track listing, which did not include "Cathy's Clown", and released it shortly after Jan Berry's crash near Deadman's Curve. Jan & Dean's cover of "Cathy's Clown" is available on the "Filet Of Soul Redux: The Rejected Master Recordings" release.

Also in 1960, the song was adapted into [[French language|French]] by [[Georges Aber]] and [[Pierre Delanoë]] as "''Le p'tit clown de ton cœur''"<ref>{{Cite web |title=Johnny Hallyday - Le p'tit clown de ton coeur - ultratop.be |url=https://www.ultratop.be/fr/song/62785/Johnny-Hallyday-Le-p'tit-clown-de-ton-coeur |access-date=2024-07-18 |website=www.ultratop.be}}</ref> (meaning "The Little Clown of your heart"), and was recorded by French [[rock and roll]] singer [[Johnny Hallyday]] and was released as the lead single off of Hallyday's second studio album ''Nous les gars, nous les filles'' ("Us guys, us girls") that November, which was released two months later.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Johnny Hallyday - LP Nous les gars, nous les filles Vogue LD 539-30 |url=https://www.hallyday.com/Son/Disco/1961/1961-02-01lpvogueld539-30nouslesgarsnouslesfillesa.html |access-date=2024-07-18 |website=www.hallyday.com}}</ref> Hallyday's version peaked at Number 48 on the French Belgian charts in early 1961.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Johnny Hallyday - Le p'tit clown de ton coeur - ultratop.be |url=https://www.ultratop.be/fr/song/62785/Johnny-Hallyday-Le-p'tit-clown-de-ton-coeur |access-date=2024-07-18 |website=www.ultratop.be}}</ref>

Also in 1960, the song was adapted into French by Georges Aber and Pierre Delanoë as "Le p'tit clown de ton cœur" (meaning "The Little Clown of your heart"), and was recorded by French rock and roll singer Johnny Hallyday and was released as the lead single off of Hallyday's second studio album Nous les gars, nous les filles ("Us guys, us girls") that November, which was released two months later. Hallyday's version peaked at Number 48 on the French Belgian charts in early 1961.

sections.heading: Other notable versions
sections.wikitext: The song was covered by [[Bill and Boyd]] in New Zealand; their version reached number 1 on the [[List of number-one singles in 1960 (New Zealand)|Lever Hit Parades]] chart in that country in July 1960.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.flavourofnz.co.nz/index.php?qpageID=Lever%20hit%20parades&qyear=1960&qmonth=Jul&qweek=21-Jul-1960#n_view_location |title=Lever hit parades: 21-Jul-1960 |work=Flavour of New Zealand }}</ref> Another cover, by the English singer Dick Jordon, reached number 5 in New Zealand.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.flavourofnz.co.nz/index.php?qpageID=Lever%20hit%20parades&qyear=1960&qmonth=Aug&qweek=11-Aug-1960#n_view_location |title=Lever hit parades: 11-Aug-1960 |work=Flavour of New Zealand }}</ref>  English musician [[John Lennon]] recorded a piano version, though only as a short demo that was never finished.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MTNDQKsOssY |title=Cathy's Clown |date= |last=John Lennon |access-date=2025-06-06 |via=YouTube}}</ref> [[Neil Sedaka]] recorded a cover version for his 1983 album "[[Come See About Me (Neil Sedaka album)|Come See About Me]]".
sections.text: The song was covered by Bill and Boyd in New Zealand; their version reached number 1 on the Lever Hit Parades chart in that country in July 1960. Another cover, by the English singer Dick Jordon, reached number 5 in New Zealand.  English musician John Lennon recorded a piano version, though only as a short demo that was never finished. Neil Sedaka recorded a cover version for his 1983 album "Come See About Me".
